title: The trade screen and what it shows
summary: A trade in TCG Card Shop Simulator runs on a screen of its own: a card panel for each side, album and buying panels, market prices and album counts on both sides, separate lines for selling, trading, haggling, declining and accepting, a price you can type, and four ways out of it.
body: A trade is a screen rather than a conversation. The screen has a card panel for you and a card panel for the customer, along with album panels and a buying panel, so both halves of a deal are visible at once instead of only one side.

The customer has things to say at each stage. There are separate sets of lines for selling, for trading, for haggling, for declining and for accepting, which is why the same customer can sound different depending on how the deal is going.
What they say animates. The line at the top of the screen belongs to the customer and has an animation of its own, so it arrives rather than simply redrawing.

The numbers are shown on both sides. There is a market price for each card and an album count for each side, so what a card is worth and how many of them you already hold are both on screen before you commit.

You set the price. The screen has a price input and a display for it, along with the price itself kept as text, so the figure you name is typed and then shown back to you rather than being chosen from a list.

It tells you which of two things is happening. Trading and selling have their own text and their own group on the right, so a customer who wants to swap cards is not presented the same way as one who wants to buy.
The graph is reachable from it. The screen holds the item price graph screen, so the history of a price can be opened while a trade is being discussed rather than before it.
There are four ways out. Accepting, cancelling, asking to think about it and finishing each have their own control, and there is a flag for presenting the newer version of the screen.

It behaves like the game's other screens. It has a group for itself, a rule about closing when another screen opens, and a check for whether the virtual keyboard is active, which is why text entry during a trade does not open a second interface on top of it.
What this entry does not tell you: what a customer will accept, how often they haggle, or how a trade's value is worked out. We have not verified those numbers, so we do not print them.

facts.claim: The screen shows a card panel for each side, album panels and a buying panel.
facts.evidence: identifiers: CustomerTradeCardScreen, m_CardUI_L, m_CardUI_R, m_CardUI_Album_L, m_CardUI_Album, m_CardUI_Buying

facts.claim: There are separate sets of customer lines for selling, trading, haggling, declining and accepting.
facts.evidence: identifiers: m_CustomerSellCardTextList, m_CustomerTradeCardTextList, m_CustomerHaggleTextList, m_CustomerDeclineTextList, m_CustomerAcceptedTextList

facts.claim: The customer's line at the top has an animation of its own.
A market price is shown for each side, along with an album count for each side.
The price is typed into an input and shown back on a display.
Trading and selling have their own text and their own group on the screen.
The item price graph screen is reachable from the trade screen.
There are separate controls for accepting, cancelling, thinking it over and finishing.
There is a flag for the newer version of the interface.
It behaves like the game's other screens, with a group, a close-when-opened rule and a check for the virtual keyboard.
The trade screen places the cards on stand locations it keeps as a group of their own.
The screens carry follow-locations of their own: a counter screen, a credit-card screen and a display-card-info screen each have one.
